strengths: Introduces PriVi, a large-scale (424h) primate-centric video pretraining dataset combining research/observational footage from 11 settings with curated YouTube data, addressing a clear gap in the animal behavior recognition literature where prior datasets are human-centric or too narrow.

Presents a scalable, well-described data curation pipeline (relevance classifier on CLIP embeddings, cut detection, zero-shot primate detection via Grounding DINO, source-dependent subsampling) that is reasonably validated (82.8% recall/90.3% precision, 95.9% ROC-AUC for relevance classifier; 82.7 mAP for zero-shot detection).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four diverse benchmark datasets (PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, ChimpBehave) spanning different settings (camera trap, zoo, drone, indoor) and species, demonstrating consistent improvements over both frozen and fully finetuned baselines, including specialized state-of-the-art models like ChimpVLM and AlphaChimp.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each dataset component (YT-Filtered vs R&O vs random YouTube), primate-centric cropping, in-domain continual pretraining, and various attentive classifier design choices (downprojection, number of layers, class tokens vs single CLS token), providing good evidence for design decisions.

The lightweight attentive classifier (220K parameters) is shown to outperform much larger classifier heads (e.g., 225x more parameters) while achieving strong results, which is a practically useful finding for low-resource behavior recognition applications.

The paper demonstrates favorable data efficiency and generalization properties, which is valuable for domains like conservation biology and ethology where labeled data is scarce and costly to acquire.
Plans to release code, models, and most of the dataset (86% of PriVi) support reproducibility, which is commendable for a data-centric contribution.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the core pretraining architecture (V-JEPA) is used with default settings without modification, and the main novelty lies in data curation and a moderately engineered classifier head, which may be seen as limited methodological innovation for a top-tier venue.

Species diversity in evaluation is narrow — only chimpanzees and baboons are represented across the four benchmark datasets, despite the pretraining set nominally covering macaques, lemurs, marmosets, and orangutans; the paper does not evaluate whether representations generalize to these underrepresented pretrained species, limiting the evidence for claimed 'general-purpose' applicability.

All experiments rely on ground-truth bounding boxes for primate-centric cropping at evaluation time (per limitations), which is a significant practical limitation not fully addressed — real-world deployment would need to pair this with a detector, and no results are shown for pipeline performance using detected (imperfect) boxes at inference/evaluation time.

Pretraining is relatively short (8 epochs, 75k steps, single continual pretraining run on top of an already pretrained V-JEPA checkpoint) and lacks a clear ablation on pretraining duration/scale, making it hard to assess whether reported gains would hold or grow with more extensive pretraining, or how sensitive results are to this choice.

Some comparisons in Table 4 are not fully apples-to-apples (e.g., AlphaChimp solves a harder joint detection+recognition task and results are the authors' own reproduction due to incompatible protocols), which weakens the strength of the state-of-the-art claims somewhat, though this is disclosed.

No confidence intervals or statistical significance testing are reported despite averaging over five classifier runs; given some of the reported gains are modest (e.g., PanAf500 Acc improvement of ~1.9 points over V-JEPA baseline in Table 4), it is unclear how robust some individual comparisons are.

The paper's claim of being a 'general-purpose' model is somewhat overstated given the restricted taxonomic scope (still limited to great apes/Old World monkeys in evaluation) and the relatively modest scale of pretraining data compared to typical foundation-model pretraining corpora.

Missing dataset entries in Table 4 (e.g., empty cells for VideoMAEv2 on PanAf500/ChimpACT, InternVideo-L on BaboonLand/ChimpBehave) reduce the completeness of baseline comparisons across all four datasets.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (424h), diverse primate-centric video dataset assembled from 11 behavioral research sources plus curated YouTube footage, addressing a genuine gap in human-centric video foundation model pretraining.

Presents a scalable, well-documented data curation pipeline (CLIP-based relevance filtering, cut detection, zero-shot primate detection, source-dependent subsampling) with quantified filter performance (82.8% recall/90.3% precision, 95.9% ROC-AUC).

Extensive empirical evaluation across four heterogeneous benchmark datasets (PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, ChimpBehave) spanning captive, semi-free, and wild settings, with consistent improvements over strong fully fine-tuned and specialist baselines.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of YouTube curation (vs. random selection), R&O data, primate-centric cropping, and classifier head design, lending credibility to individual design choices.

The lightweight frozen attentive classifier (220K params) is a practically useful contribution, showing strong performance with far fewer trainable parameters than comparable attentive-head baselines (e.g., 225x fewer than V-JEPA2-style heads).
Plans to release code, models, and most of the dataset, supporting reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: 14% of the pretraining data (camera-trap footage) cannot be released, and the released dataset's species composition is dominated by macaques while almost all downstream evaluation is on chimpanzees and baboons, raising questions about how representative the curated set is relative to what is actually validated.

Evaluation relies on ground-truth bounding boxes for primate localization in all four benchmarks, which is acknowledged as a limitation but substantially weakens claims of real-world/in-the-wild applicability, since a practical pipeline would need to rely on automatic (noisier) detections for the actual recognition task, not just for pretraining-time cropping.

Comparisons to baselines are not uniformly rigorous: AlphaChimp numbers are self-reproduced due to incompatible protocols, and some baseline results are left blank/missing in Table 4 (e.g., VideoMAEv2 and InternVideo-L on several datasets), making the completeness and fairness of the SOTA comparison harder to assess.

Results are somewhat inconsistent with the paper's own narrative: e.g., PriVi-only pretraining slightly underperforms the V-JEPA baseline on BaboonLand balanced accuracy (33.99 vs 34.57), and in-domain continual pretraining sometimes hurts other metrics (e.g., PanAf500 Acc drops from 86.74 to 85.01 after CID), which is not clearly discussed despite the paper's claim that "PriVi contributes across all datasets."

No variance/uncertainty is reported for the main results in Table 4 (comparison to prior SOTA), only for internal ablations (5 classifiers averaged), making it hard to judge whether reported gains over baselines are statistically meaningful, especially on small datasets like ChimpBehave and BaboonLand.

The technical contribution is primarily a data curation and engineering effort layered on existing components (V-JEPA, CLIP, Grounding DINO); no comparison is provided isolating whether gains stem from the proposed data vs. simply from more primate-centric video regardless of curation details, nor is there a comparison with other SSL backbones pretrained on the same data to show the result generalizes beyond V-JEPA.

Species and setting diversity, while an improvement over prior single-dataset efforts, is still limited to 11 source settings, and the paper's claim to be "general-purpose" for primate behavior is not yet tested on primate taxa beyond chimpanzees/baboons, limiting demonstrated generalization claims made in the title and abstract.

strengths: Introduces PriVi, a large-scale (424h) primate-centric video pretraining dataset combining curated research/observational data across 11 settings with filtered YouTube footage — a genuinely useful resource for a data-scarce domain, addressing a real gap (existing video foundation models are human-centric).

The data curation pipeline (CLIP-based relevance classifier, cut detection, zero-shot primate detection via Grounding DINO, source-dependent subsampling) is well-motivated, clearly described, and validated with reasonable held-out metrics (82.8% recall/90.3% precision, 95.9% ROC-AUC for relevance filtering; 82.7 mAP for detection).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four diverse benchmark datasets (ChimpACT, BaboonLand, PanAf500, ChimpBehave) covering different settings (zoo, drone, camera trap) and species, with consistent improvements over strong specialized/finetuned baselines despite using only a lightweight frozen classifier (220K parameters).

Thorough and informative ablations: dataset composition (YT-Filtered vs R&O vs random YouTube vs PriVi), in-domain continual pretraining, primate-centric cropping, and multiple attentive-classifier design choices (downprojection, number of layers, class tokens) — each isolating a clear source of improvement.

The proposed lightweight attentive classifier is a nice practical contribution, achieving competitive/better performance than heavier classifier heads used in V-JEPA/V-JEPA2 with far fewer parameters, which is valuable for the low-label regime relevant to this application.

The paper is transparent about limitations (11 source settings, only chimpanzees/baboons evaluated, use of ground-truth bounding boxes) and commits to releasing code, models, and most of the dataset, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: A substantial portion of the pretraining data (14%) and some baselines' comparisons are not fully reproducible/shareable, and the evaluation protocol for AlphaChimp is explicitly a self-reproduction due to incompatible protocols (Table 4), which slightly weakens the head-to-head SOTA comparison claims.

All experiments rely on ground-truth bounding boxes for cropping at both pretraining/continual-pretraining and evaluation time (the paper notes zero-shot detection is used for continual pretraining, but final evaluation numbers use GT boxes) — this limits claims about real-world, fully automated deployment where detections would need to be used end-to-end.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it primarily combines existing components (V-JEPA, CLIP-based filtering, Grounding DINO, standard classifier-head design choices) rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithms; the novelty rests mainly on the dataset curation and empirical demonstration of domain-specific pretraining benefits.

Species coverage skews heavily toward chimpanzees and macaques with limited representation of other primate taxa (e.g., very few orangutan/lemur samples achieve robust coverage), and evaluation is restricted to chimpanzees and baboons only, so claims of broad 'general-purpose' primate modeling are not fully substantiated across the primate order.

Some results are mixed rather than uniformly positive (e.g., PriVi+CID underperforms PriVi alone on PanAf500 Acc in Table 4, and B-Acc drops for ChimpACT+PanAf500 continual pretraining in Table 3), which the paper does not deeply discuss or explain.

The paper lacks compute/inference cost comparisons and details on scalability of the curation pipeline to even larger, more diverse pretraining corpora, leaving open questions about how the approach would generalize with more data or additional primate taxa/settings.
